items.readable_text:
Content:
The midpoint theorem states the following:

Content:
> The line segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side, and its length is equal to half the length of the third side.

Content:
To illustrate, consider the triangle [MATH: \triangle ABC] shown below, where [MATH: M] is the midpoint of [MATH: \overline{AB}] and [MATH: L] is the midpoint of [MATH: \overline{AC}.] How can we find the length of [MATH: \color{SteelBlue}{\overline{BC}}] if [MATH: {\color{DarkGoldenrod}{ML}} = 4?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/197641f478abe12da442d31f8009dc24]

Content:
According to the midpoint theorem, since [MATH: \overline{LM}] joins the midpoints of the two sides [MATH: \overline{AB}] and [MATH: \overline{AC},] the length of [MATH: \overline{LM}] is half the length of the third side [MATH: \overline{BC}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {\color{DarkGoldenrod}{ML}} =\dfrac{1}{2}{ \color{SteelBlue}{{BC}}}]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: {\color{SteelBlue}{BC}} = 2 {\color{DarkGoldenrod}{ML}} =2\cdot 4 = 8.]

Content:
Note that the midpoint theorem also guarantees that [MATH: \overline{ML} \parallel \overline{BC},] even though we didn't need to use that fact to solve this particular problem.
